question: Progressive vs stable MCI (conversion to AD) among ADNI MCI participants, predicted from structural MRI. Same task, same population class, same channel (MRI). Allowed differences: follow-up window (at least 18 months vs pMCI described as progressing within three years), input (one baseline hippocampal box vs whole-brain axial slices from two time points), training target (AD/CN transfer vs direct pMCI/sMCI training), architecture and unit of analysis.
metric: Accuracy with accuracy (75.85% vs 84.74%) and AUC with AUC (0.777 vs 0.8587). P-122 scores longitudinal samples (823 samples from 275 subjects, about 3 per subject), P-182 scores subjects. The metric type is the same; the uncertainty below uses subjects as n.

figures.P-122: Held-out test: Acc 0.8474, AUC 0.8587 on 124 longitudinal samples; the number of test subjects is not reported (about 41 if the 823/275 ratio holds). Wilson on 41 subjects 0.708-0.927; on 124 samples 0.774-0.900. Six-fold CV over all 275 subjects (121 pMCI, 154 sMCI): mean Acc 0.8428 (fold SD 1.65), Wilson with n=275: 0.795-0.881; mean AUC 0.8599 (fold SD 0.0167), Hanley-McNeil with n1=121, n2=154: SE 0.0236, 95% CI 0.814-0.906.
figures.comparison: P-122's 0.8474 (test) and 0.8428 (CV) both lie outside P-182's Wilson interval 0.713-0.799, and P-182's 0.7585 lies outside P-122's CV interval 0.795-0.881 (it lies inside the wide test-set interval computed on about 41 subjects). For AUC, P-122's 0.8587/0.8599 lie outside P-182's 0.723-0.831 and P-182's 0.777 lies outside P-122's CV interval 0.814-0.906. The rule's test (one estimate outside the other's 95% interval) is met, and on the CV figures it is met in both directions.

matched_figure_check: Neither paper reports a result under the other's input condition: P-122 has no single-scan result and P-182 has no two-time-point result, so no matched figure reconciles the pair. However, P-122's own experiments on its data, input and horizon vary only the architecture: the unimproved Eff-GCNet backbone gives Acc 71.6%, AUC 0.7770 (Table 4), and classical backbones with its multi-scale attention give 75.5-81.4%, AUC 0.78-0.88 (Table 3). These bracket P-182's 75.85% and reproduce its AUC of 0.777. This is paper-internal evidence that the architecture difference alone can produce a gap of this size (13 points inside P-122 vs 8.9 points between the papers). The ablation uses P-122's own backbones, not P-182's model, and rests on the same held-out test of 124 samples (Wilson on 124 samples for 71.6%: 0.631-0.788; on about 41 subjects: 0.564-0.831). Whether this counts as a paper showing that one candidate explanation is sufficient, which the rule treats as a condition-3 failure, is the judgment left open.
performance_validity: Passes condition 5: 0.8474/0.8587 (P-122) and 0.7585/0.777 (P-182) are below 0.97, checked in both PDFs. P-182's 94.07%/0.993 is the AD-vs-CN training fold, not the compared figure.

candidate_explanations.difference: Architecture. P-122's own ablation moves accuracy from 71.6% (AUC 0.777) to 84.7% on its data by adding its multi-scale attention and adaptive fusion modules. This is the explanation P-122 comes closest to showing sufficient; it is shown for P-122's backbones, not for P-182's model.
candidate_explanations.quote: The performance of the spatiotemporal attention module is evaluated using the unimproved Eff-GCNet, which in this configuration without any improvement or add-on blocks

candidate_explanations.difference: Input representation: two time points of whole-brain axial slices (P-122) vs one baseline 3D hippocampal box (P-182). Not shown to be sufficient: P-122 reports no single-time-point result.
candidate_explanations.quote: The architecture synthesizes longitudinal sMRI data from dual temporal points

candidate_explanations.difference: Input region: P-182 uses only a 3D box around the hippocampus.
candidate_explanations.quote: the model utilizes voxel intensity values from a 3D bounding box surrounding the entire hippocampal region

candidate_explanations.difference: Training target: P-182 trains on AD vs CN and applies the model to MCI without MCI-label training; P-122 trains directly on pMCI/sMCI.
candidate_explanations.quote: the model was trained to first differentiate AD and CN (data source: ADNI-2/GO), with the assumption that these two extreme classes would allow the model to learn the necessary representations for classifying MCI subjects as well.

candidate_explanations.difference: Label definition and window: P-182 labels on evaluations at least 18 months apart and excludes 65 reverters; P-122 describes pMCI as progressing within three years, with selection guided by DSM-5 criteria.
candidate_explanations.quote: This dataset was labeled as either stable MCI (sMCI) or progressive MCI (pMCI) based on longitudinal diagnostic evaluations obtained at least 18 months apart.

candidate_explanations.difference: Unit of analysis and validation: P-122 scores longitudinal samples (about 3 per subject) on a 15% held-out split and six-fold CV; P-182 scores 381 subjects once.
candidate_explanations.quote: For the sMCI group, we gathered 449 longitudinal samples from 154 subjects diagnosed with sMCI. Similarly, the pMCI group consisted of 374 longitudinal samples from 121 subjects

reason: The pair meets conditions 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6. Both papers classify pMCI vs sMCI in ADNI from structural MRI, and P-122's accuracy (84.7% test, 84.3% CV over 275 subjects) lies outside P-182's Wilson interval of 71.3-79.9% (n=381), with the AUCs separated in the same way. No figure is reported under the other paper's input condition. But P-122's own ablation on its data puts its unimproved backbone at 71.6% with AUC 0.777, the same level as P-182, so the gap follows P-122's architecture modules. Whether a within-paper ablation against the paper's own backbone counts as a paper showing the explanation sufficient (a condition-3 failure) is the operator's call.
